items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; the item reports finite experimental observations and source scope.
items.statement:
Zheng et al.'s InverseBench reports 14 plug-and-play diffusion-prior algorithms and domain-specific baselines on five selected cases: first-Born optical scattering, raw multi-coil knee MRI, black-hole very-long-baseline interferometry, full waveform inversion, and two-dimensional vorticity-form Navier–Stokes inversion. For these experiments, the authors report that diffusion-prior methods often outperform conventional baselines when the training data are suitable, while a classical full-waveform-inversion optimizer initialized from a smoothed ground truth outperforms the tested diffusion-prior methods. In cases with closed-form forward models, methods using more forward-gradient queries can be more accurate and more expensive; the paper reports that this trend fails for its numerical PDE cases. Its Navier–Stokes split has one validation case and ten test cases. The paper reports step-size/Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy (CFL) failures in its PDE experiments. Its Figure 5 out-of-distribution diagnostics feed digit images to a black-hole prior trained on simulated black-hole images, and nine-cell scattering sources to a prior trained on one-to-six-cell sources; for the black-hole case, the authors report outputs with the prior's characteristic ring feature. These are empirical observations for the named data, solvers, methods, tuning protocol, and hardware; they establish no universal ranking, stability bound, posterior exactness, risk-transfer bound, or robustness theorem.

There is a first-Born notation discrepancy between the paper and its released implementation. Appendix B.1 defines a contrast-dependent total field and then displays a sensor equation with that field multiplied by the contrast, which does not itself exhibit a fixed linear map. The pinned implementation instead passes the fixed incident field into the sensor-propagation routine and constructs its cached linear matrix from that fixed field. This page therefore identifies the implemented benchmark as the first-Born linear case and does not infer linearity from the printed contrast-dependent expression.

references.title: Hongkai Zheng et al., InverseBench: Benchmarking Plug-and-Play Diffusion Priors for Inverse Problems in Physical Sciences, ICLR 2025, full paper and appendices
references.locator: §4.1, PDF p. 6, and Appendix B.1, PDF pp. 22–23: 128×128 first-Born optical-scattering setup, fixed physical dimensions, 20 transmitters, receiver counts 360/180/60, and train/validation/test split. Appendix A.1, Table 3: measurement-noise level $\sigma_y=10^{-4}$.

references.locator: Lines 326–445: fixed incident field is passed to `full_propagate_to_sensor`; the cached matrix is formed from that field and the sensor Green function.

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; the finite real contrast grid and fixed measurement operators are explicit inputs.
items.statement:
In the implemented first-Born optical-scattering benchmark, the unknown is a real $128\times128$ array $z$ of cellwise permittivity contrasts, each equal to the object's permittivity minus the background permittivity. For each transmitter $j\in\{1,\dots,20\}$, $u_{\rm in}^{(j)}$ is its fixed incident illumination field, and $H_{m,r}$ is the fixed Green response from cell $r$ to receiver $m$. The released forward implementation reports measurements

$$y_{j,m}=\Delta x\Delta y\sum_r z_r\,\overline{u_{\rm in}^{(j)}(r)}\,H_{m,r}+e_{j,m},$$

where $m$ indexes receivers, $r$ indexes grid cells, $\Delta x=\Delta y=18\,\mathrm{cm}/128$ are the grid spacings, and $e$ is additive Gaussian measurement noise with reported level $\sigma_y=10^{-4}$. Thus the implemented map is real-linear in $z$. The reported physical field is $18\,\mathrm{cm}\times18\,\mathrm{cm}$, the wavelength is $0.84\,\mathrm{cm}$, the background permittivity is $1$, and the receiver count is $360$, $180$, or $60$. The paper reports $10{,}000$ training images of HL60-cell permittivity, $10$ validation images, and $100$ test images; it curates the test samples so their cosine similarities to training images are below $0.6$, where cosine similarity of nonzero image arrays $a,b$ is $\langle a,b\rangle/(\|a\|_2\|b\|_2)$. The paper's Appendix B.1 also prints a contrast-dependent total-field formula; this example follows the fixed-incident-field implementation and does not infer linearity from that printed formula.

items.title: Multi-coil MRI benchmark

references.title: Hongkai Zheng et al., InverseBench: Benchmarking Plug-and-Play Diffusion Priors for Inverse Problems in Physical Sciences, ICLR 2025, full paper and appendices
references.locator: §4.1, PDF p. 7, and Appendix B.2, PDF pp. 23–24: fastMRI raw knee data, ESPIRiT sensitivity maps, 320×320 preprocessing, and training/tuning/test counts; Table 4, PDF p. 20, reports metrics over 94 test cases.

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; the finite coil operators and image data split are supplied inputs.
items.statement:
In the InverseBench multi-coil knee MRI case, a complex image $z\in\mathbb C^n$ with $n=320^2$ produces one k-space data vector per receiver coil:

$$y_j=PFS_jz+n_j\in\mathbb C^m,\qquad j=1,\ldots,J.$$

Here $J$ is the number of coils, $S_j$ is multiplication by the sensitivity map of coil $j$, estimated for each slice using ESPIRiT as implemented in SigPy, $F$ is the discrete Fourier transform, k-space is the Fourier-coefficient data space, $P\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}$ selects the acquired k-space entries, and $n_j$ is the raw measurement noise in that coil. With these operators fixed, the measurement map is linear in $z$; the paper does not assume Gaussian noise for the raw-data benchmark. Its fastMRI knee split contains $25{,}012$ training images, $6$ hyperparameter-search images, and $94$ test images, preprocessed to $320\times320$. For the reported metrics in Tables 4 and 5, the reference ground-truth image is the magnitude image of the minimum-variance unbiased estimator (MVUE); these magnitude-MVUE images are also used as training ground truths for Residual UNet and E2E-VarNet. The reported test metrics include peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity index measure (SSIM), and data misfit.

references.title: InverseBench source implementation, pinned revision 1db5932bc2995504491663d1e2c498e7317c5404, inverse_problems/blackhole.py
references.locator: Lines 110–140: baseline-orientation flags and ordered triangle/quadrangle indices; lines 208–233: complex-conjugation correction and closure-phase argument; lines 241–260: ordered log-closure-amplitude ratio.

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; the finite telescope, image, and sample sets are supplied inputs.
items.statement:
In the InverseBench black-hole-imaging case, very-long-baseline interferometry correlates telescope electric-field signals to produce complex visibilities of a nonnegative source-brightness image $z(\rho,\delta)$ on angular coordinates $(\rho,\delta)$. For a telescope pair $(a,b)$ at time $t$, the ideal visibility is the corresponding Fourier sample

$$I^t_{a,b}(z)=\iint z(\rho,\delta)e^{-2\pi i(u^t_{a,b}\rho+v^t_{a,b}\delta)}\,d\rho\,d\delta,$$

where $(u^t_{a,b},v^t_{a,b})$ is the projected baseline. The observed visibility is

$$V^t_{a,b}=g^t_ag^t_be^{-i(\phi^t_a-\phi^t_b)}I^t_{a,b}(z)+\eta^t_{a,b},$$

where $g^t_a,g^t_b$ are telescope amplitude gains, $\phi^t_a,\phi^t_b$ are phase errors, and $\eta^t_{a,b}$ is additive Gaussian thermal noise. For an oriented telescope triangle $(a,b,c)$, the closure phase is $\arg(V^t_{a,b}V^t_{b,c}V^t_{c,a})$; when a stored visibility has the opposite baseline orientation, the implementation uses its complex conjugate. For the ordered quadrangle $(a,b,c,d)$ returned by the implementation's closure-amplitude routine, the log closure amplitude is $\log\!\bigl(|V^t_{a,b}||V^t_{c,d}|/(|V^t_{a,d}||V^t_{b,c}|)\bigr)$. The closure phase is defined only when its triangle product is nonzero, and a log closure amplitude is defined only when all four relevant visibility amplitudes are nonzero. No value is assigned by these formulas at an undefined zero visibility; this domain restriction does not assert an implementation masking or rejection rule. The benchmark also uses total flux $\iint z(\rho,\delta)\,d\rho\,d\delta$. These derived data are nonlinear functions of the visibilities, so their noise is not additive. The training images are $50{,}000$ simulated general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic images resized to $64\times64$. Because those images are not public, the paper generates $5$ validation and $100$ test images from a pretrained diffusion model. The sparse, nonconvex closure-data model has multiple solutions compatible with the observations; the reported tests do not make a general uniqueness or posterior-calibration claim.

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; the finite discretization, source signals, and solver are supplied inputs.
items.statement:
In the InverseBench full-waveform-inversion (FWI) case, the unknown $v(x)>0$ is the compressional-wave velocity on a two-dimensional physical domain $\Omega$; its discretization is a $128\times128$ velocity map $z$. For each source signal $q(x,t)$, the pressure field starts with zero initial pressure and velocity, $u(\cdot,0)=0$ and $\partial_tu(\cdot,0)=0$ on $\Omega$, and solves

$$v(x)^{-2}\,\partial_t^2u(x,t)-\nabla^2u(x,t)=q(x,t),$$

and the observation is the receiver restriction $y=Pu$, where $P$ samples the wavefield at the selected receivers. The benchmark uses a $2.54\,\mathrm{km}\times1.27\,\mathrm{km}$ domain, horizontal and vertical grid spacings of $20\,\mathrm m$ and $10\,\mathrm m$, a $0.001\,\mathrm s$ time step chosen to satisfy the numerical solver's Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy stability condition, a $5\,\mathrm{Hz}$ Ricker source wavelet, and $1\,\mathrm s$ of simulated time. Its top boundary has the natural free-surface condition, while the other boundaries have absorbing conditions of width $80$ grid points. It uses $16$ sources at depth $1270\,\mathrm m$ and $129$ receivers evenly placed near the free surface at depth $10\,\mathrm m$. The reported observation noise is zero. The CurveFaultB velocity-map split has $50{,}000$ training maps, one validation map, and ten test maps, resized to $128\times128$. These counts and solver settings define this empirical benchmark instance; they are not existence or convergence claims for full waveform inversion.

items.title: Two-dimensional Navier–Stokes benchmark

references.title: Hongkai Zheng et al., InverseBench: Benchmarking Plug-and-Play Diffusion Priors for Inverse Problems in Physical Sciences, ICLR 2025, full paper and appendices
references.locator: §3, PDF pp. 5–6; §4.1, PDF p. 7; Appendix B.5, PDF pp. 26–27; Tables 2 and 8, PDF pp. 5 and 21: vorticity model, pseudo-spectral solver, noise/gradient access, and split counts.

references.title: InverseBench source implementation, pinned revision 1db5932bc2995504491663d1e2c498e7317c5404, inverse_problems/navier_stokes.py
references.locator: Lines 47–106 define the Laplacian, inverse, dealiased zero-mode mask and streamfunction velocity; lines 129–170 retain the state zero mode during time stepping; ForwardNavierStokes2d at lines 179–243 supplies forcing, target, evolution and subsampling. This implementation does not establish a mean-zero dataset-generation law.

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; the finite periodic grid, random-field data generation, and numerical solver are supplied inputs.
items.statement:
In the InverseBench two-dimensional Navier–Stokes case, the spatial domain is the periodic square $(0,2\pi)^2$ (the flat torus). In the physical vorticity model, the periodic velocity $u(x,t)\in\mathbb R^2$ is divergence-free and its scalar curl is $\omega=\partial_1u_2-\partial_2u_1$. This curl has zero spatial mean. Taking the spatial mean of $u$ to be zero fixes the constant-velocity ambiguity. For viscosity $\nu>0$, forcing $f(x)=-4\cos(4x_2)$, and compatible initial curl $\omega_0$, the physical model is

$$\partial_t\omega+u\cdot\nabla\omega=\nu\Delta\omega+f,\qquad \nabla\cdot u=0,\qquad \omega(\cdot,0)=\omega_0.$$

The released benchmark uses a finite-grid scalar state denoted $w$. Its pinned solver computes velocity by Fourier streamfunction derivatives, which select zero spatial mean velocity and ignore the constant Fourier mode of the scalar state. The nonlinear term uses a dealiased state with zero mode removed, while the time-update formula retains the original state's zero mode; the specified forcing also has zero mean. Thus the solver defines a scalar-state extension even when $\overline w\ne0$. One must not identify such an entire state with the curl of a periodic velocity. In the corresponding continuum mean-split convention, $w=\overline w+\omega$, $-\Delta\psi=\omega$, and $u=(\partial_2\psi,-\partial_1\psi)$; only $\omega=w-\overline w$ is the curl, and $\overline w$ is a conserved scalar offset. This convention explains the zero-mode distinction; it does not assert that the finite-grid dealiased scheme is an exact continuum solution or that the released dataset has been projected to zero mean.

The reconstruction target is the supplied dataset field $z=w_0$ used as initial state for the inversion solver; the observation is $y=PL(z)+n$, where $L$ is this numerical scalar-state solution map over the specified inversion horizon $T$, $P$ samples the final field, and $n$ is Gaussian measurement noise. The dataset-generation horizon is a separate five time units: §4.1 and Appendix B.5 report independent Gaussian seed fields $\xi\sim\mathcal N(0,(-\Delta+9I)^{-4})$, evolved under the stated forcing for five time units to produce the dataset of nontrivial initial fields. Accordingly, $z$ denotes the evolved field, not a claim that the inversion-input distribution remains Gaussian with the seed covariance. On the full periodic space the reported covariance gives the constant eigenmode variance $9^{-4}>0$; the paper does not specify a zero-mode projection for the seed law. The scalar-state implementation permits retaining that offset without asserting the incompatible identity $w=\nabla\times u$ for arbitrary seeds.

InverseBench uses a pseudo-spectral solver with adaptive time stepping; the reported setup has a $128\times128$ grid, Reynolds number $200$, $10{,}000$ training samples, one validation sample, and ten test samples. The paper reports black-box forward access without a closed-form gradient for this implementation; the one-validation/ten-test split is part of this empirical benchmark, not a population-level guarantee.

items.title: Prior-matched and out-of-distribution cases

references.title: Hongkai Zheng et al., InverseBench: Benchmarking Plug-and-Play Diffusion Priors for Inverse Problems in Physical Sciences, ICLR 2025, full paper and appendices
references.locator: §4.1, PDF pp. 6–7: task-specific training/test sets; §4.3 and Figure 5, PDF pp. 9–10: black-hole digit and nine-cell inverse-scattering out-of-distribution cases; Appendix C, PDF pp. 28–29: prior-mismatch discussion and scope.

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; the empirical training and test splits are supplied finite datasets.
items.statement: For an operational within-source reference, InverseBench trains its multi-coil MRI diffusion prior on $25{,}012$ fastMRI knee images and evaluates on $94$ held-out images from the same named data collection. This is a dataset-family match, not a claim that the population training and test laws are equal. Its separate out-of-distribution diagnostics change the source: a black-hole-imaging prior is trained on $50{,}000$ simulated general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic images, while one stress test uses digit images; in linear inverse scattering, the prior is trained on sources with one through six cells, while the stress test uses nine-cell sources. The paper reports outputs drawn toward black-hole structure in the digit case and more effective recovery when the scattering source is close to the trained prior. These are finite, method- and dataset-specific observations; they provide no risk bound or distribution-shift guarantee.

items.title: A solver-invalid FWI iterate

references.title: Hongkai Zheng et al., InverseBench: Benchmarking Plug-and-Play Diffusion Priors for Inverse Problems in Physical Sciences, ICLR 2025, full paper and appendices
references.locator: §4.3 and Figure 3, PDF pp. 8–9: DAPS step-size sensitivity and a reported FWI velocity map that violates the PDE solver's CFL condition; Appendix B.4, PDF p. 26: the particular FWI discretization and stable time step.

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used; the example applies a supplied solver-specific admissibility predicate to one finite trial.
items.statement: Fix an FWI velocity-model solver $\mathcal S$ with a declared finite admissibility predicate $\operatorname{adm}_{\mathcal S}(v)$ that checks that solver's coefficient, boundary, mesh, and time-step conditions, including its solver-specific Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy (CFL) condition. If an optimization method proposes a candidate velocity map $\widetilde v$ with $\operatorname{adm}_{\mathcal S}(\widetilde v)=\mathrm{false}$, the benchmark records the call as a solver/admissibility failure; its evaluation protocol specifies whether and how that failed trial contributes to any numerical aggregate. In its FWI DAPS experiment, InverseBench reports that a smaller learning rate gave numerically stable but data-ineffective outputs, while a slightly larger learning rate produced a noisy velocity map that violated the PDE solver's CFL condition and failed. The paper gives no exact violating iterate or universal CFL threshold; this example claims neither.
